messages.subject: Re: Occupancy vs Detection Probability
messages.subject_clean: Occupancy vs Detection Probability
messages.body_plain:
You can look at detection probability as a "nuisance" parameter. Ultimately, the parameter of interest is occupancy, but in order to estimate occupancy with accuracy, we have to take into account how effectively the species of interest can be detected. This is why detection probability should be approached first--it actually impacts your estimates of occupancy.

For example, a site surveyed for three seasons with three surveys in each season might appear:

101  000  001

If we could detect the species with 100% accuracy, we'd say that the site went extinct from year 1 to year 2. However, we know from seasons 1 and 3 that the species was present at the site, but not always detected (indicated by zeros). Clearly, detection probability is not 100%. Therefore it is possible that during year 2, the species was actually present (occupancy), but undetected (detection). This probability is directly incorporated into the calculation of occupancy probability.

Therefore, occupancy probability is an informed estimate of occupancy after taking into account detectability. Detection probability is a nuisance parameter that is determined from the 1's and 0's of your survey history.

This is a pretty basic concept--it might be helpful for you to read some of the Mackenzie papers from the early 2000s, and the text Occupancy Estimation and Modeling.

Mackenzie et al. 2002 <http://www.uvm.edu/rsenr/vtcfwru/spreadsheets/occupancy/Occupancy%20Exercises/Exercise3/MacKenzie%20et%20al.%20single-season.pdf>
Mackenzie et al. 2003 <http://www.esajournals.org/doi/pdf/10.1890/02-3090>

> Hey there
>
> I have run an analysis with unmarked in R. I will post my results soon but first I wanted some help understanding some theory. I have a simple question - what is the difference between the probability of detection and the probability of occupancy?
>
> The way I understand it is that the probability of detection is the probability of detecting/finding/catching/seeing/hearing/sampling your study organism at a particular site. The probability of occupancy is the probability of your study organism actually being at a particular site even though you didn't detect/find/catch/see/hear or sample it.
>
> I study bats and investigate activity at sites using acoustic sampling. Often, species are not recorded on site because of limitations of the equipment even though they may actually be present on site. Therefore, if my knowledge is correct, the probability of detection would tell me the probability that I may record bats using my acoustic equipment based on covariates and the probability of occupancy would tell me the probability that a bat would be a site based on covariates?
>
> Am I getting the right picture here?
>
> Thanks
> Jon

A long time ago, I compared colext() vs PRESENCE vs BUGS using simulated data, and I found very similar results. However, I didn't simulate data with tons of missing values and parameters near boundaries, as you have in your data. Anyone want to do more extensive simulation tests?

You could also try using PRESENCE's estimates as starting values in colext. This might indicate if there are real differences or if one of the programs has failed to find the global minimum.

Dear Brittany,

I have a couple of general comments on the choice of "the best method for analysis". I feel that the choice of an analytical method depends on at least three things: ecology, sample design and biology of your species, and available analytical resources.
(1) To decide what is the best method to analyse a set of data you must start from the ecological question. Without a clear idea of "why" you want to do an analysis, there is no way to say what analysis is best or even adequate. I see this as the same thing as the "why-what-how" progression of questions in monitoring (Yoccoz et al, TREE, 2001).
(2) Even if you want to analyse your data a certain way, perhaps your data were not collected such that you can reasonably make the assumptions implicit in the use of a certain model, or, the way how your species behaves (for instance, moves in space and time) does not match the assumptions of the model.
(3) The best possible method may not be within your reach because the model or the fitting may be too complicated for you to understand, for instance, if you'd have to code up some complicated MCMC algorithm.
Consideration of all three aspects may lead you to conclude that a certain model is best for your question, your design/your species and for your resources. In some cases, it may even lead to the conclusion that no reasonable analysis is possible for your data set.

More specifically, in your case, you seem to be interested in spatial and potentially temporal patterns in a bird population around a lake, and you worry about imperfect detection, hence you use the mixed models in unmarked rather than those you can fit in lme4, for instance. Ideally, you might analyse the counts and model abundance, but in the bittern case, with max counts of one, you can do occupancy with hardly any loss of information.

One important assumption for occupancy models is closure: that the state of occurrence of a site ("species present" or "species absent") does not change over the duration of your sampling. With a large number of occasions, this assumption is always suspect, and with your sampling extending over 3 years, is bound to be violated so strongly, in my opinion, to make the analysis meaningless.

So you must account for the openness of the system, by considering a dynamic occupancy model perhaps (function colext) or, if you want to model counts for estimation of abundance, use dynamic N-mixture models (i.e., the Dail-Madsen model, pcountOpen). Remember that the closure assumption is (much) more difficult to meet when modeling abundance, rather than occurrence, because a change in the abundance state from one occasion to another from 8 to say 7, means a violation of the closure assumption when modeling abundance, but not when modeling occurrence (i.e., occupancy).

However, in your case, with such sparse data (15 bittern detections  or so ?), using the more complex dynamic model (with more params to estimate) would "dilute" the little information you have so much more that it would most likely fail as well for numerical reasons.

So in my opinion, for the bittern, you just don't have enough data to do any reasonable modeling in unmarked, and you should take other species with (many) more observed birds.

(((Or, some people (actually many) would simply forget about modeling measurement errors (= 1 minus detection prob) and model the observed occurrence using some kind of logistic regression perhaps. This approach comes with a couple of important hidden assumptions, which may or may not screw your inference, and you simply don't know it: (1) detection is perfect or (2) detection is not perfect but at least does not vary along desired dimensions of comparisons, e.g., does not vary much between habitat types along the lake, which you are interested in comparing.)))

Kind regards --  Marc

Hi - so another question about predictSE.zip -  I've used predictSE.zip to get predictions and standard errors for the my pcount ZIP models and I calculated my confidence intervals by multiplying the SEs by 1.96 and adding them to or subtracting them from the prediction...However, I recently realized that estimated confidence intervals for similar models in programs such as PRESENCE are calculated by first multiplying the log scale standard errors by 1.96, adding this to the log scale mean and THEN transforming the result.  I'm not sure if what I've done is sufficient despite these differences, or if there is another method out there?  I tried re-transforming the SE and prediction output of "predictSE.zip" but that made the confidence intervals look a little out of wack....any suggestions?

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] pcount, predictions of abundance, and superpopulations...
messages.body_plain:
hi Kaylan,

 The predictions from the various types of N-mixture models (including pcount) provide estimates of E(N) at the site level (local population size). These only have a clear interpretation, strictly speaking, when the local populations are closed. The best way to make sense of this is suppose you were sampling wetland basins for duck brooks and you could imagine, over a short time, that N is well defined and constant for a particular wetland basin.
 For counts of landbirds the definition of N is imprecise because you can't define the actual area being sampled.  The best case interpretation is that it is the population of individuals exposed to sampling at the site.

 Thats about as exact as I can be.   See Kery (2010 Introduction to WinBUGS book) chapter 21 for a basic discussion (in the context of Bayesian analysis).

 The reason we usually call this a superpopulation size is because when sampling is done repeatedly over time (days) then this N includes not only all individuals that were instantaneously available during a particular sample but also any individuals whose homeranges overlap the count area.

 The model does allow direct predictions to be made of N at sites that you don't predict, using the predict() function for example (and examples in the unmarked documentation and workshop materials).   So if you count on a sample of sites and want to predict to a landscape then this can be done, and has been done many times. We have a couple examples in the workshop materials here

https://sites.google.com/site/unmarkedinfo/home/workshops/patux2012/slides

In particular, see these two lectures:

Slides_Multimix.pdf

slides-distsamp-intro.pdf

Neither of them are exactly the N-mixture model (pcount) but the mechanics of doing the prediction in unmarked would be exactly the same.

regards
andy

messages.subject_clean: potential bug in predict(fm, "det"...) when appendData=T
messages.body_plain:
Dear Group,

Trying to reproduce the Chisq value returned from parboot() in the pb@t0 slot, I believe I stumbled upon a bug in the appendData=T option when using predict(fm, type="det").

My pcount model is of double-observer data, and p was modeled to vary between observer1 and observer2.  The predict function returns a vector of p-hats that is length 2 x R, where R is the number of double-samples (or sites).

When the option appendData is set TRUE, a duplicate copy of the model data is appended vertically, ie: df.out= cbind( p.hat ( rbind( fm@data, fm@data )).  The "bug" is that the p-hats are ordered: p1, p2, p1, p2, p1, p2,...etc.  Therefore, the p-hats from predict do not align with the rows of appended data, except for p1 in the first row of the data.frame.

I learned this by approaching my computation of expected counts, similarly to the excellent dialogue and examples presented in this discussion: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/Chisq/unmarked/9AU01DVzel8/hvmU0agNfa4J

Borrowing from that discussion, I modified Doug's code as follows:

expected.counts= function(fm){
  R = dim(getY(fm@data))[1]

  predict.state= predict(fm, 'state')[,1]
  predict.det= predict(fm, 'det')[,1]

  p1.hat= predict.det[1:R]
  p2.hat= predict.det[(R+1):(R*2)]

  expected= data.frame(y1.hat= predict.state*p1.hat,
                         y2.hat= predict.state*p2.hat)
  return(expected)
}

E.ct= expected.counts(FD2_m3_full3)
O.ct= getY(FD2_m3_full3@data)
(Chisq= sum((E.ct - O.ct)^2/E.ct))

The computed Chisq value was much, much larger than the value returned in the t0 slot of my parboot object.

Interestingly, when I computed the expected counts as,  E.ct = fitted(fm), the computed Chisq statistic matched that of the parboot object.

On a hunch, based on the ordering of obsCovs extracted from the umf, I modified my expected.counts function so that:

p1.hat= predict.det[seq(1,(2*R),2)]
p2.hat= predict.det[seq(2,(2*R),2)]

and, the resultant Chisq statistic then matched the output of the t0 slot of my parboot object.

Just wanted to mention this, in case it saves somebody else some headache in the future.  I also want to thank the participants in the linked discussion, because that was helpful for a discussion I was having with work colleagues today.

Best,
Ted

Hi Doug,

Based on my recent experience, I don't think you are indexing your predicted p's correctly.  Try substituting your estimated detection parameter breakout like:

  predict.det1 <- predict.det[seq(1,(3*n),3)]
  predict.det2 <- predict.det[seq(2,(3*n),3)]
  predict.det3 <- predict.det[seq(3,(3*n),3)]

I believe your predicted p's are returned in order: p1,p2,p3,p1,p2,p3,p1,p2,p3, etc.

Other's raise an interesting point with respect to the psi parameter.  However, given Richard's note that psi is not incorporated into the values returned by the fitted() function, I suspect my suggested correction for indexing p1, p2, and p3, will yield results equal to the expected count values returned with fitted(), which I think are correct (except for the unaccounted psi parameter).

For more detail on the ordering issue with predict, see my recent post: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/unmarked/btt41S-d6kc

I appreciate the high quality of discussion in this post, and your clear, concise examples.

Thanks,
Ted

You can’t use them in the way you do, because, as you see, this will sometimes result in inadmissible values >1. Perhaps somebody else can explain what these SE’s mean.

In all cases, the linear modeling in both parts of the occupancy model (detection, occupancy) takes place on the logit scale. I think that I would generally use the predict function to get estimates of occupancy for your model on the probability scale, along with 95% Cis. Then, you can report these or plot them, for a model with covariates.

On Fri, Mar 28, 2014 at 6:45 PM, Ted Jones <salmo...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Dear Group,
>
> Trying to reproduce the Chisq value returned from parboot() in the pb@t0 slot, I believe I stumbled upon a bug in the appendData=T option when using predict(fm, type="det").
>
> My pcount model is of double-observer data, and p was modeled to vary between observer1 and observer2.  The predict function returns a vector of p-hats that is length 2 x R, where R is the number of double-samples (or sites).
>
> When the option appendData is set TRUE, a duplicate copy of the model data is appended vertically, ie: df.out= cbind( p.hat ( rbind( fm@data, fm@data )).  The "bug" is that the p-hats are ordered: p1, p2, p1, p2, p1, p2,...etc.  Therefore, the p-hats from predict do not align with the rows of appended data, except for p1 in the first row of the data.frame.
>
> I learned this by approaching my computation of expected counts, similarly to the excellent dialogue and examples presented in this discussion: https://groups.google.com/forum/#!searchin/unmarked/Chisq/unmarked/9AU01DVzel8/hvmU0agNfa4J
>
> Borrowing from that discussion, I modified Doug's code as follows:
>
> expected.counts= function(fm){
>   R = dim(getY(fm@data))[1]
>
>   predict.state= predict(fm, 'state')[,1]
>   predict.det= predict(fm, 'det')[,1]
>
>   p1.hat= predict.det[1:R]
>   p2.hat= predict.det[(R+1):(R*2)]
>
>   expected= data.frame(y1.hat= predict.state*p1.hat,
>                          y2.hat= predict.state*p2.hat)
>   return(expected)
> }
>
> E.ct= expected.counts(FD2_m3_full3)
> O.ct= getY(FD2_m3_full3@data)
> (Chisq= sum((E.ct - O.ct)^2/E.ct))
>
> The computed Chisq value was much, much larger than the value returned in the t0 slot of my parboot object.
>
> Interestingly, when I computed the expected counts as,  E.ct = fitted(fm), the computed Chisq statistic matched that of the parboot object.
>
> On a hunch, based on the ordering of obsCovs extracted from the umf, I modified my expected.counts function so that:
>
> p1.hat= predict.det[seq(1,(2*R),2)]
> p2.hat= predict.det[seq(2,(2*R),2)]
>
> and, the resultant Chisq statistic then matched the output of the t0 slot of my parboot object.
>
> Just wanted to mention this, in case it saves somebody else some headache in the future.  I also want to thank the participants in the linked discussion, because that was helpful for a discussion I was having with work colleagues today.
>
> Best,
